演奏時將琴一端置於膝上，另一端置於地面或支架，亦可使用兩支架；琴身擺放使高音弦位: One end of the instrument rests on the knee and the other on the floor or a stand; two stands may also be used. The body is placed so that the high strings are at the front right, and all the strings are plucked only to the right of the bridge. The right hand plucks with the fingernails, or, by style, with the fingers or a plectrum; the left hand presses the strings to change pitch and can also play the bass strings. A beginner should first tune with the hidden tuning device on the right, then move the bridge for fine tuning; pressing to the left of the bridge raises the pitch by more than a semitone. Notation can be in numbers, the highest string being 1 and the rest numbered in order; if the do–re–mi–so–la pentatonic scale is used, string 1 is re. Some contemporary players prefer a horsehair bow to a plectrum.
雅託格琴是蒙古傳統撥弦齊特琴，屬弦鳴樂器。琴身為長木箱，一端向下傾斜，尺寸、調音: The yatga is a traditional Mongolian plucked zither, a chordophone. Its body is a long wooden box with one end sloping down, and its size, tuning, number of strings and bridges can vary; the modern instrument commonly has twenty-one strings and measures 1.62 metres overall, and there is also a thirteen-string version. When playing, one end rests on the knee and the other on the floor or a stand; the right hand plucks with the fingernails and the left presses the strings to change pitch, and the bass strings can also be played. It is used in court, aristocratic, folk, contemporary classical and film music.
雅託格琴源自中國古箏，後在蒙古發展為傳統彈撥齊特琴。歷史上，十二弦版本因十二根弦: The yatga comes from the Chinese guzheng and later developed in Mongolia into a traditional plucked zither. Historically the twelve-string version was used for royalty, since twelve strings corresponded to court rank; the ten-string version was for commoners, and more than twelve strings was reserved for court and temple. In the traditional Mongolian epic Janggar, a young princess plays a yatga of eight hundred strings and eighty-two bridges, using only the seven bridges below.
雅託格琴琴體由細長木製盒子構成，主要採用蒙古地區的優質木材，如椴木或松木作為共鳴: The body of the yatga is a long, slender wooden box, using good Mongolian woods such as lime or pine for the resonating box. Its strings are usually gut or modern nylon, ten to twelve of them. The bridge is of wood or bone and carries and transmits the vibration of the strings. The nut is also of wood or ivory. The whole structure is simple and fully expresses Mongolian craft.
雅託格琴音色明亮清透，具有典型的撥弦樂器特質。其高音區呈現清脆、穿透力強的音響，: The yatga has a bright, clear timbre, with the qualities typical of a plucked instrument. In the high register the sound is crisp and carries well, with a metallic sheen, while the low register is warm and full, with deep resonance. The slender wooden body resonates effectively, which gives the timbre its distinctive warmth and bleakness. Compared with the gorgeous elegance of the guzheng, the yatga is rougher and plainer; compared with the harp it has more of an Eastern spirit and national character. Its range is wide and the registers are clearly separated, so it can present both light, nimble melodic lines and the vast mood of the Mongolian steppe. The polyphony produced by the two hands working together makes the whole sound more expressive and more moving.
